bull_thesis:
The bullish case rests on one genuine, verifiable claim: this company owns the actual bottleneck in the current electronics upcycle, and the numbers already show it. Kingboard Laminates is the world's largest producer of copper-clad laminate, the fibreglass-and-copper sheet that every printed circuit board is built on. What makes it unusual is that it does not buy its raw materials so much as make them: it produces its own copper foil, glass yarn, glass fabric, epoxy resin and bleached kraft paper. In a cycle where the scarce items are electronic-grade glass fabric and high-specification, low-loss laminate for artificial-intelligence server hardware, an integrated producer captures the margin of the entire chain rather than paying it away to suppliers. A competitor buying glass fabric on the spot market during a shortage simply cannot match that cost position, and new fabric capacity takes years to build.

The evidence that this is working is in the reported halves, not in a story. Gross margin has expanded sequentially across three consecutive reporting periods: 15.9% in the second half of 2024, 18.4% in the first half of 2025, 20.6% in the second half of 2025. Net income in the second half of 2025 was HK$1.51 billion against HK$598 million a year earlier, a rise of 152%. Full-year 2025 revenue grew 10% to HK$20.40 billion and earnings per share rose 81% to HK$0.78. Then, on 30 July 2026, the company issued a positive profit alert stating that first-half 2026 profit would be more than triple the year-earlier figure, which implies something above HK$2.8 billion earned in six months, more than the whole of 2025. This is an inflection with a visible slope, not a single lucky period.

The balance sheet lets the company play the cycle rather than survive it. Borrowings of HK$4.63 billion against HK$2.88 billion of cash and short-term investments leaves net debt of roughly HK$1.75 billion, under one turn of trailing operating profit before depreciation. The solvency score (Altman-Z of 9.5) and the accounting-quality checklist (Piotroski 7 of 9) both confirm there is no financial distress question here and no refinancing cliff.

The bull's valuation claim is that the market is looking at the wrong earnings number. On the last reported annual figure of HK$0.78 the shares look expensive at fifty times. On the forward estimates, they do not: the five analysts covering the name model 2026 revenue of about HK$35.4 billion and average earnings per share of HK$2.58, rising to HK$3.50 in 2027 and HK$4.18 in 2028. At HK$38.70 that is fifteen times this year, eleven times next year and nine times the year after. If the artificial-intelligence build-out is a multi-year capital cycle rather than a two-year spike, and if the shift toward high-specification grades is a permanent mix improvement rather than a price blip, then a company earning HK$3.50 a share deserves more than eleven times, and the shares are worth double today's price.

The conditions this case depends on, stated plainly so they can be falsified: first, that high-speed laminate demand keeps growing through 2027 and 2028 rather than pausing when the first wave of data-centre orders is filled; second, that the glass-fabric and high-specification laminate shortage persists long enough that competitor capacity arriving in 2027-28 does not collapse pricing; third, that the mix shift toward specialty grades is durable enough to hold gross margin above the 20% level rather than reverting to the mid-teens; and fourth, that the poor cash conversion of 2025 proves to be an upcycle working-capital drain that unwinds, rather than a permanent feature of how this company sells.
bear_thesis:
The bearish case does not dispute a single number in the bull case. It disputes what those numbers are worth, and it rests on this company's own recent history rather than on any speculation.

Start with the precedent, because it is decisive. In 2021 Kingboard Laminates earned HK$6.78 billion on revenue of HK$28.80 billion, with gross margin above 34% and earnings per share of HK$2.17. That was the previous mania in laminate pricing. By the second half of 2022, six months after the peak, gross margin had fallen from roughly 30% to 12% and half-year net income had collapsed to HK$83 million. By 2023 full-year net income was HK$907 million and earnings per share were HK$0.29 — an 87% decline from the peak in two years. Nothing structural changed in between. Same plants, same vertical integration into glass and copper and resin, same management, same customers. What changed was the price of laminate. This company has already run the experiment the bull is proposing, and the answer is on file.

Against that precedent, look at what is being paid today. At HK$38.70 the equity is valued at about HK$122 billion, with enterprise value of roughly HK$124 billion once the HK$1.75 billion of net debt is added. That is about fifty times the last reported annual earnings, seven and a half times book value of HK$5.20 a share, and — the comparison that should stop a committee — roughly two and a half times the market value this same company commanded at the top of its last cycle, when it was actually earning HK$6.78 billion. The current consensus only expects it to earn HK$6.64 billion this year. In other words, the market is paying two and a half times the previous peak valuation for a business the street expects to merely match its previous peak profit.

The consensus itself will not bear the weight being put on it. Four analysts supply the 2026 earnings estimate, and their range is HK$1.25 to HK$3.74 a share — the highest is three times the lowest. For 2027 the range is HK$1.45 to HK$5.42, nearly four times. An average drawn from that distribution is not a forecast; it is a record of profound disagreement about where in the cycle we are. Underwriting at the average means underwriting a number no individual analyst actually holds. At the low end of the 2026 range the shares trade at thirty-one times, not fifteen.

The forensic quality of the earnings is the second problem. Reported 2025 net income was HK$2.44 billion, but cash generated from operations across the two halves was only about HK$1.20 billion — roughly half. After HK$1.28 billion of capital spending, free cash flow for the year was approximately negative HK$80 million. The mechanism is receivables: HK$9.21 billion outstanding at 31 December 2025 against HK$20.40 billion of annual revenue, about 165 days of sales, and up HK$1.83 billion in the second half alone — more than that half's entire net profit. Every dollar of the profit improvement, and then some, went into customer credit rather than the bank. Meanwhile the HK$1.93 billion dividend paid in 2025 was funded not from that year's cash generation but from the balance sheet, alongside HK$901 million of new short-term borrowing. A business whose profits do not convert to cash at the top of its cycle has a receivables book that is a risk, not an asset, when the cycle turns and customers come under pressure.

The third problem is the market environment. The dominant shared driver of this entire trade is artificial-intelligence capital spending, which is also the single most crowded macro factor in the current tape. The market has already begun to discriminate within that complex on the basis of free cash flow rather than revenue growth, and this company generated none in its last reported year. The share price itself has voted: HK$104.20 on 25 June 2026 to HK$29.14 on 30 July, a 72% loss in five weeks, followed by a violent chop between HK$29 and HK$42, with more than 9% of the entire free float trading on an average day. That is not a shareholder register that provides support at any particular level. With only 29% of the 3.15 billion shares in public hands and average daily volume of 83 million, this is a momentum battleground.

What would confirm the bear case: half-year results in late August that show the profit tripling as promised but with receivables extending further and operating cash flow still lagging profit; commentary or industry data showing new glass-fabric and high-specification laminate capacity being commissioned in China through 2027; a second-half order book that flattens rather than accelerates; or gross margin peaking below the 30% level the company reached in 2021, which would confirm that this cycle is smaller than the last one while the valuation assumes it is larger.
consensus_delta:
Where we disagree with the market is not about the earnings. It is about what those earnings are.

The street's position, expressed in the numbers, is that Kingboard Laminates earns about HK$2.58 a share in 2026, HK$3.50 in 2027 and HK$4.18 in 2028, and the twelve-month analyst target of HK$51.66 says those forecasts deserve roughly fifteen times. Read the chain of assumptions that requires: that this year's profit level is a base to grow from rather than a peak to fall from; that the shortage in electronic-grade glass fabric and high-specification laminate persists for at least three more years; and that a commodity substrate producer should carry a mid-teens multiple on peak earnings.

We think the first assumption is where the error sits, and this company's own accounts contain the refutation. In 2021 it earned HK$2.17 a share with gross margin above 34%. Eighteen months later, in the second half of 2022, half-year profit was HK$83 million and gross margin was 12%. By 2023, earnings per share were HK$0.29. Nothing structural changed — the same plants, the same vertical integration into glass, copper and resin, the same customers. Only the price of laminate changed. The street is currently modelling 2028 earnings per share of HK$4.18, which would be nearly double the highest annual figure this business has ever produced, at a point in the cycle when new capacity in exactly the bottleneck products is being financed. The historical response time for Chinese materials capacity is two to three years, which lands precisely on the 2028 forecast.

The second disagreement is about the consensus itself, and it is a disagreement about epistemics rather than about laminate. Four analysts supply the 2026 earnings estimate and their range is HK$1.25 to HK$3.74; for 2027 it is HK$1.45 to HK$5.42. When the highest estimate is three to four times the lowest, the average is not a forecast, it is a summary of confusion. Anyone underwriting at fifteen times the average is underwriting a number no individual analyst holds. At the low end of the 2026 range, today's price is thirty-one times earnings.

The third disagreement, and the one the current tape cares about most, is about cash. The market is valuing this company on reported profit. Reported 2025 net income was HK$2.44 billion; cash generated from operations was about HK$1.20 billion; after HK$1.28 billion of capital spending, free cash flow was approximately negative HK$80 million. Receivables of HK$9.21 billion represent about 165 days of sales and grew HK$1.83 billion in the second half of 2025 alone — more than that half's entire net income. The current market regime has explicitly begun to sort the artificial-intelligence complex on free cash flow rather than revenue growth, punishing the capital-spending payers while rewarding the cash generators. On that test this company scores badly, and we do not believe that is yet in the price.

Where we agree with the market, and it matters: the near-term earnings are going to be excellent, the margin inflection across three consecutive reported halves is real, and the vertical integration into glass fabric is a genuine advantage rather than a marketing line. We are not calling this a bad business. We are calling it a good business at a price that already assumes the best case.
forcing_function:
The dated event is the half-year results for the six months to 30 June 2026, due on or before 31 August 2026 under the Hong Kong listing rules and, by reference to last year's 23 August publication, most likely within the next week or two. It was pre-flagged by a positive profit alert dated 30 July 2026 stating that first-half profit would be more than triple the year-earlier HK$933 million.

But the honest assessment is that this event is unlikely to force a re-rating in our favour, because it is a catalyst for a thesis we do not hold. The magnitude has already been disclosed, and the shares have already risen 33% from their 30 July low in anticipation. What the announcement will genuinely reveal, and what nobody outside the company currently knows, are four things: the interim dividend, whether operating cash flow finally converted a reasonable share of the reported profit, whether the receivables balance extended beyond 165 days of sales, and any commentary on the second-half order book and on the product mix between commodity and high-specification grades. Those are the disclosures that would move our view, and three of the four could plausibly move it further against the stock rather than toward it.

The event that would actually force the re-rating this valuation implies is a slower one, and it is a de-rating rather than a re-rating: the arrival, most likely through 2027, of new Chinese capacity in electronic-grade glass fabric and high-specification laminate, and the consequent normalisation of the pricing that has produced the current margin expansion. The industry's historical capacity response time is two to three years from the onset of a shortage, which lands on the period the current consensus expects to be the strongest. There is no single dated announcement for that; it arrives as a sequence of reported half-years in which the margin stops improving. That is the eighteen-month horizon on which our base case sits.

One further consideration under this book's rules on independence of drivers. The resolution driver for this entire thesis — artificial-intelligence capital spending — is the single most dominant shared macro factor in the current market, and the regime framework requires that concentration in one such factor be enforced against rather than accumulated. Whatever forces this stock's next move, it will very likely be the same thing that moves every other name in that complex on the same day, which is precisely the kind of exposure this book is meant to avoid stacking.
valley_of_death:
The risky window here is unusual, because the near-term news is likely to be good and the risk is that good news is not enough.

Within two weeks, on or before 31 August 2026, the half-year results arrive. They will almost certainly show profit more than tripling, because the company said so on 30 July. The specific danger is that the market has already paid for that: the shares have risen 33% from their 30 July low of HK$29.14 to today's HK$38.70 on precisely this expectation. The most likely near-term disappointment is not the headline but the quality beneath it — an operating cash-flow line that again converts only about half of reported profit, a receivables balance extending beyond the 165 days already on the books, or a smaller-than-hoped interim dividend given that the 2025 payout of HK$1.93 billion already exceeded that year's free cash flow and was accompanied by HK$901 million of new short-term borrowing. Any of those would confirm the bear's core forensic point at exactly the moment sentiment is most stretched.

Over the following three to nine months the harder problem arrives. This is a business with a working-capital hump, not a cash-burn hump: in an upcycle where both volumes and prices rise, receivables and inventory absorb cash faster than profit produces it. That is precisely what happened in 2025, and 2026's much larger revenue base will make it worse in absolute terms. Capital spending is also running above depreciation — HK$1.28 billion against roughly HK$1.0 billion of depreciation in 2025, a ratio of about 1.37 — because the company is adding the capacity the shortage justifies. The combination means free cash flow can stay negative through a boom, and the dividend can only be sustained by borrowing against it. There is no maturity wall and no solvency question; net debt is under one turn of operating profit before depreciation and the solvency score is 9.5. But a company that cannot self-fund its dividend at the top of its cycle has no cash cushion to deploy when the cycle turns.

The macro overlay is the sharpest near-term risk. The current regime read describes a market in which the artificial-intelligence complex has split in half, with the capital-spending payers being destroyed while a narrow set of component suppliers melts up, and in which free cash flow rather than revenue has become the discriminator. It also warns explicitly that the recent promotion of freshly crashed names as an attractive hunting ground rests on selection of the three winners of a two-week window, with no accounting for the crashes that simply kept crashing. This name is a freshly crashed, negative-free-cash-flow, artificial-intelligence-capital-spending supply-chain stock. It sits on the wrong side of every one of those distinctions. Separately, the regime notes the September rate decision now carries roughly a 30-34% probability of a hike and zero probability of a cut through December; a higher-for-longer path is not friendly to a stock trading at fifty times trailing earnings.

Finally, the sheer volatility is itself a risk to any position taken now. In the last five weeks the shares have moved from HK$104.20 (25 June) to HK$29.14 (30 July), then chopped between HK$29 and HK$42, including a 9% gain on 17 August immediately followed by an 8% fall on 18 August. A position sized as though this were an ordinary industrial holding would be sized wrong by a wide margin.
positioning_washout:
The shareholder register here is the opposite of the yield-focused, passive base this question usually contemplates, and that changes the answer entirely.

Only about 29% of the 3.15 billion shares are in public hands — roughly 923 million shares — with the balance held by Jamplan (BVI) Limited, the holding vehicle of the wider Kingboard group. Average daily volume is about 83 million shares, and through the crash it ran between 100 million and 250 million a day, peaking at 318 million on 17 June. On a typical day, in other words, roughly 9% of the entire free float changes hands; on the worst days, more than a quarter of it. That is not an investment register. It is a trading venue.

The practical consequence is that there is no mechanical forced-selling event to wait for, because the forced selling has already happened and it happens continuously. The 72% collapse from HK$104.20 on 25 June to HK$29.14 on 30 July, in five weeks and on enormous volume, was the wash-out. Anyone who was going to be liquidated by margin calls or momentum-strategy stop-outs has largely been liquidated. What remains is a fast-turning base of traders positioned around the half-year results, and that base provides no support at any particular price — it will not defend HK$38, and it did not defend HK$60 or HK$80 on the way down.

This matters for how the committee should think about the entry level. In a normal deep-value situation you can wait for a capitulation and buy the last seller. Here, the capitulation already came and went in July and the shares are 33% above that low, so waiting for the flush is waiting for something that has already occurred. The flush that would actually create an opportunity is a second, valuation-driven de-rating rather than a positioning-driven one — the kind that arrives when the earnings are still rising but the multiple stops being paid, which is what happened to this company through 2022. That is a slower and less dramatic process than a five-week collapse, and it does not announce itself with a volume spike.

One structural point cuts the other way and should be acknowledged. A 29% free float in a name with a genuine thematic story is a squeeze mechanism. There is very little stock available relative to the demand a theme can generate, which is a large part of why the shares went from HK$10.50 to HK$107.20 in the first place. The same mechanism can run again on a strong interim print. That is a reason to expect further violent upside episodes; it is not a reason to own the shares at a price above our estimate of what the business is worth.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now, at conviction 2, and we are inheriting that call from our own decision of 10 August rather than re-deriving it, because nothing dated has happened in the business since then that would justify changing it. The half-year results have still not been published, the 30 July profit alert remains the most recent company statement, and the only thing that has moved is the price — HK$35.72 then, HK$38.70 now. A higher price on unchanged facts makes the case slightly worse.

Let us be precise about what we are and are not saying, because the temptation to read this as a bearish view of the company would be a misreading. This is a good business having a genuinely good year. Kingboard Laminates is the world's largest maker of copper-clad laminate, the fibreglass-and-copper sheet underneath every printed circuit board, and it is unusual in that it makes its own copper foil, glass yarn, glass fabric and resin rather than buying them. In a cycle where electronic-grade glass fabric is the scarce item, that integration is worth real money, and the accounts show it: gross margin has expanded across three consecutive reported halves, from 15.9% to 18.4% to 20.6%, and second-half 2025 profit rose 152% year on year. The company told the market in writing on 30 July 2026 that first-half 2026 profit would be more than triple the prior year. The balance sheet is genuinely conservative — net debt of about HK$1.75 billion is under one turn of operating profit before depreciation, and the solvency score of 9.5 leaves no financial distress question. Our forensic review scored management's credibility at 3 out of 5 and the business trajectory as strengthening, with a narrow but real cost moat that is stable rather than widening, and no structural force threatening the company's long-term existence.

Our objection is entirely about price, and it comes down to one comparison. At HK$38.70 the market values this equity at about HK$122 billion. At the top of its last cycle in 2021, when it actually earned HK$6.78 billion — a figure the street only expects it to match this year — the same company was worth roughly two-fifths of that. We are being asked to pay two and a half times the previous peak valuation for a business expected to merely match its previous peak profit, in an industry whose last peak was followed by an 87% earnings collapse within two years on an unchanged asset base. Valuing the business by its parts, we get to about HK$22 a share: roughly HK$22.00 from the laminates and upstream materials operations on normalised earnings of HK$2.20 a share at ten times, plus about HK$0.40 for the property and long-term investment portfolio marked down for Chinese property weakness, less about HK$0.56 for net debt. Our adverse case is HK$12 and our favourable case is HK$49. The price today sits above our base case and below our best case, which is the worst possible place to be underwriting: no margin of safety, and roughly two and a half times as much distance to the adverse case as to the favourable one. There is no structural floor to catch a fall — no net cash, no deal terms, no tender, and a book value of HK$5.20 that is nowhere near the price.

Three things reinforce the call. First, the earnings do not convert to cash: 2025 profit of HK$2.44 billion produced about HK$1.20 billion of operating cash flow and, after capital spending, roughly negative HK$80 million of free cash flow, with receivables at 165 days of sales and the dividend part-funded by new borrowing. The current market regime has begun sorting this entire complex on free cash flow rather than revenue, and on that test this name fails. Second, the analyst consensus being used to justify the price is unusable — four analysts with a 2026 estimate range of HK$1.25 to HK$3.74 a share are not forecasting, they are disagreeing, and at the low end today's price is thirty-one times earnings. Third, the resolution driver is artificial-intelligence capital spending, the single most crowded shared macro factor in this tape, and our own framework requires us to enforce independence of drivers rather than accumulate exposure to that one. The regime document also warns, in its own words, that the recent enthusiasm for freshly crashed names rests on selecting the winners of a two-week window without accounting for the crashes that kept crashing. This name is a freshly crashed, negative-cash-flow, artificial-intelligence-supply-chain stock; it is the exact profile that warning was written about.

We have deliberately not let the upcoming half-year announcement move the score in either direction. Under this book's rules the timing of a corporate event is descriptive, not a conviction lever — the dated-event portfolio is run separately — so what we are judging here is the residual value case, and that case is unattractive at HK$38.70 regardless of what happens on 31 August. By the same token we are not penalising the name for the fact that the profit figure has already been pre-announced.

What would change our mind, stated as a level rather than a hope: a price in the low twenties or below, which would put the shares at our base-case value with the operating momentum still intact, or evidence in the interim results and the following period that cash conversion has genuinely normalised — operating cash flow at or above reported profit and receivables days falling meaningfully below 150 — which would let us raise normalised earnings and the multiple together. Absent one of those, this is a business we admire at a price we decline.

# Forensic Dossier — Kingboard Laminates Holdings (1888.HK)

*Prepared 18 August 2026. Price used throughout: HK$38.70, the live Hong Kong quote on 18 August 2026 (down 8.1% on the day from a previous close of HK$42.12), sourced from the market-data feed. All figures are in Hong Kong dollars unless stated.*

**An unusual note on sources, stated up front so the reader can weigh everything that follows.** Kingboard Laminates does not hold quarterly earnings calls, and no earnings-call transcript exists for this company in our licensed transcript database — the provider returns nothing for this ticker. This dossier therefore cannot do what it normally does: track the drift of management's spoken language across eight quarters. There is no spoken record to track. What exists instead is a sparse, twice-yearly written disclosure record — Hong Kong issuers report half-yearly, not quarterly — plus the audited numbers themselves. I have built the dossier from the financial statements, the balance sheet, the cash-flow statement, the analyst estimate set, and the trading record. Where I quote management, I quote only what our own committee recorded from the company's written filings; I have invented nothing. Where I could not verify something this session, I say so plainly rather than dressing an assumption as a fact.

**What the company is.** Kingboard Laminates is the world's largest maker of copper-clad laminate — the fibreglass-and-copper sheet that every printed circuit board is built on. It is unusual in that it does not buy its raw materials so much as make them: the company also produces copper foil, glass yarn, glass fabric, epoxy resin and bleached kraft paper, the inputs that go into the laminate. It also owns a portfolio of commercial, residential and industrial investment property, trades copper, and runs a hotel. It is a subsidiary of Jamplan (BVI) Limited, the holding vehicle of the wider Kingboard group, and only about 29% of its 3.15 billion shares are in public hands.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Because there is no call transcript, the "narrative" here has to be read from the reported numbers and from the company's written announcements. Read that way, the arc across the last five years is one of the cleanest boom-bust-boom shapes in the Hong Kong industrial universe.

**2021 — the previous mania.** Revenue HK$28.80 billion, net income HK$6.78 billion, earnings per share HK$2.17. Gross margin ran above 34% in both halves (HK$4.72 billion of gross profit on HK$13.92 billion of first-half revenue). This was the post-pandemic electronics restock, when laminate prices spiked and an integrated producer captured the whole chain.

**2022–2023 — the bust.** The story did not soften; it broke. Second-half 2022 net income collapsed to HK$83 million, from HK$1.83 billion in the first half of that year, as gross margin fell from roughly 30% to 12%. Full-year 2023 net income was HK$907 million against HK$6.78 billion two years earlier — an 87% decline. Earnings per share went from HK$2.17 to HK$0.29. Revenue fell from HK$28.80 billion to HK$16.75 billion. The important detail for anyone underwriting today's story: **nothing structural changed about this company between 2021 and 2023.** The same plants, the same integration, the same management. What changed was the price of laminate.

**2024 — the floor.** Revenue HK$18.54 billion, net income HK$1.33 billion, earnings per share HK$0.43. The second half of 2024 was the weakest margin period of the recovery, at 15.9% gross.

**2025 — the inflection, visible and real.** Revenue HK$20.40 billion (+10%), net income HK$2.44 billion (+81% on earnings per share). Crucially, the shape within the year is what matters: gross margin went 15.9% in the second half of 2024, to 18.4% in the first half of 2025, to 20.6% in the second half of 2025. Second-half 2025 net income of HK$1.51 billion was 152% above the HK$598 million of the year-earlier half. This is a genuine, sequentially improving inflection, not a single lumpy quarter.

**2026 — the story becomes an artificial-intelligence story.** The demand driver that the market has attached to this name is the build-out of AI server hardware, which needs high-speed, low-loss laminate — a higher-specification, higher-priced product than the commodity grades — and which has run into a shortage of electronic-grade glass fabric and yarn. Kingboard Laminates makes its own glass fabric and yarn. On 30 July 2026 the company issued a positive profit alert stating that first-half 2026 profit would be more than triple the year-earlier figure; that alert is recorded in our own committee's file from earlier this month, and I flag that I was unable to re-verify it against the exchange's filing archive in this session (the company's investor-relations site refused connection, and three financial-news sources returned errors or blocks). More than triple the first half of 2025's HK$933 million implies something above HK$2.8 billion in six months — more, in half a year, than the company earned in all of 2025.

**The thesis shift to watch.** The story has quietly migrated from "cyclical materials producer that mints cash at the top of the laminate cycle" to "structurally advantaged supplier of a scarce AI input." Those are very different claims and they carry very different multiples. The first deserves a single-digit multiple of peak earnings. The second deserves a growth multiple. Nothing in the reported financial record yet distinguishes between them, because a demand-driven price spike and a structural re-rating look identical for the first two years.

---

| Profitability is at a structurally new level | Gross margin at 20.6% is still well below the 30–34% the same company ran in 2021 and the 12% it ran in late 2022. Short-term borrowings rose HK$901 million in the same period | **Diverges.** The dividend was funded from the balance sheet, not from the year's cash generation. |

**The receivables problem, which deserves its own paragraph.** Trade and other receivables stood at HK$9.21 billion at 31 December 2025, against full-year revenue of HK$20.40 billion. That is roughly 165 days of sales outstanding — the company is waiting more than five months, on average, to be paid. Receivables rose HK$1.83 billion in the second half of 2025 alone, which is more than the HK$1.51 billion of profit reported in that same half. Put plainly: every dollar of the second-half profit increase, and then some, went out the door into customer credit rather than into the bank. Some of this is structural for a Hong Kong group with related-party trading arrangements, and some of it is the normal working-capital drain of a genuine upcycle — when volumes and prices both rise, receivables rise faster than profit. But 165 days is a long time, and it is the single number I would most want explained at the interim results.

**On the screener's valuation fields.** The scan reports a "fair value" of HK$1.15 and a discounted-cash-flow value of HK$0.30 against a HK$38.70 price, and a margin of safety of −100% on all five models. These are artefacts, not analysis: every one of those models divides by free cash flow, and free cash flow for 2025 was approximately zero. They should be disregarded entirely. Equally, the scan's line "trailing twelve-month diluted earnings per share 1.20" does not reconcile — the two reported halves of 2025 sum to HK$0.78, and the market-data provider's own trailing earnings yield of 2.01% on a HK$122 billion market value confirms HK$0.78, not HK$1.20. I have used HK$0.78 as the last reported annual figure.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Rising — but on a very thin evidentiary base, and the reader should discount this section accordingly.**

There is no spoken record. What can be observed is *disclosure behaviour*, and it has changed in one meaningful way: a company that reports twice a year and offers no guidance chose, on 30 July 2026, to pre-announce the direction and rough magnitude of its half-year result. Hong Kong issuers must disclose price-sensitive information promptly, so a positive profit alert of that size is partly a compliance act rather than a voluntary display of confidence. Still, management elected to quantify it ("more than triple") rather than issue a bare statement. That is an offensive posture, not a defensive one.

Against that, note what has *not* changed: the company still gives no forward guidance, holds no analyst calls, publishes no order-book figures, and discloses no segment-level margin detail beyond the statutory minimum. An intelligent newcomer should understand what this means practically — for a business now being valued on a demand story about AI servers, **the market has almost no company-provided information with which to test that story between reporting dates.** That information vacuum is exactly why the share price can travel from HK$10.50 to HK$107.20 and back to HK$38.70 inside twelve months.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability score: Medium — and the score is limited by the near-total absence of guidance to score.**

There is no guidance track record to audit, because the company does not guide. What can be checked is whether the one forward statement it did make points the same way as the observable trend, and it does: a profit alert in late July 2026 saying first-half profit more than tripled is directionally consistent with the margin sequence already visible in the reported halves (15.9% → 18.4% → 20.6% gross), with copper-clad laminate pricing having tightened, and with the second half of 2025 already delivering +152% year-on-year profit growth. Management is not making a claim the financials contradict.

There is also no sandbagging pattern to detect, and no beat-rate to reconcile — the analyst estimate history shows only three to five analysts covering the name, with a single analyst supplying the earnings estimate as recently as 2024. Consensus for 2025 was HK$0.72 against HK$0.78 delivered: a modest beat, on almost no coverage.

**The one thing that should temper confidence.** Analyst estimates for this name have been revised violently upward during the boom and now carry an implausible spread. For the 2026 financial year, five analysts model revenue between HK$28.1 billion and HK$43.4 billion, and four model earnings per share between HK$1.25 and HK$3.74. The high estimate is three times the low. For 2027 the spread is HK$1.45 to HK$5.42 — nearly four times. A consensus with that dispersion is not a forecast; it is a record of disagreement about where in the cycle we are. Any valuation that leans on the average of that range is leaning on a number no individual analyst actually believes.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Without calls there is no question-and-answer record. But the unanswered questions can be inferred from what the disclosures conspicuously omit, and each of them is load-bearing:

1. **How much of the margin gain is price and how much is mix?** If it is the high-speed, low-loss grades genuinely taking share of the sales mix, the gain is durable. If it is commodity laminate pricing plus a glass-fabric squeeze, it reverses when capacity arrives. The company discloses neither product-level revenue nor product-level margin, so nobody outside the company can tell.
2. **Why is cash conversion so poor at the very moment profitability is best?** Half of 2025's reported profit did not appear as operating cash. Receivables at 165 days of sales is the mechanism; the explanation is not disclosed.
3. **What is the counterparty concentration in that receivables book, and how much is with related parties inside the wider Kingboard group?** Not disclosed at a level an outside investor can assess.
4. **What capacity is being added by competitors in glass fabric and high-specification laminate?** This is the question that decides the entire thesis, and it is not a question the company can be expected to answer honestly about its own rivals.
5. **What is the dividend policy now?** The 2025 payout of HK$1.93 billion exceeded the year's free cash flow and was accompanied by HK$901 million of new short-term borrowing.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Free cash flow of approximately negative HK$80 million in 2025** against HK$2.44 billion of reported net income (full year 2025). Cash conversion of roughly 0.49 — half of profit reaches the operating cash line.

🔴 **Receivables of HK$9.21 billion at 31 December 2025, about 165 days of sales**, having grown HK$1.83 billion in the second half of 2025 — more than that half's entire net income.

🔴 **The 2025 dividend was part-funded by new borrowing** (HK$1.93 billion paid; short-term debt up HK$901 million; free cash flow negative).

🔴 **The 2022–2023 precedent.** The same asset base, with the same vertical integration, saw earnings per share fall from HK$2.17 to HK$0.29 in two years. This company has already demonstrated what its downcycle looks like, and it is severe.

🔴 **Five-year compound trends are negative despite the recovery**: book value per share −3.8% a year, earnings per share −22.6% a year over five years. The 2025 rebound has not yet recovered the 2021 base.

🔴 **A free float of only 29%** (923 million of 3.15 billion shares) against average daily volume of about 83 million shares. More than 9% of the entire free float changes hands on a typical day. This is a momentum battleground, not a stable shareholder register.

🟢 **The margin inflection is real and sequential** — gross margin 15.9% → 18.4% → 20.6% across three consecutive reported halves, with second-half 2025 net income up 152% year on year.

🟢 **Genuine vertical integration into the actual bottleneck.** The scarce inputs in the current cycle are electronic-grade glass fabric and yarn, and the company makes its own. This is not a marketing claim; it is in the asset base.

🟢 **A conservative balance sheet.** Net debt of about HK$1.75 billion against roughly HK$3.6 billion of trailing operating profit before depreciation; Altman-Z of 9.5; current ratio 1.92. There is no solvency question here and no refinancing cliff. The company can survive a downcycle comfortably — the question is only what it earns in one.

🟢 **A Piotroski score of 7 out of 9** — the accounting-quality checklist is mostly passing, and the failures are the cash-flow ones already named.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The trading record is itself a signal, and it is the loudest one available.** Over the twelve months to today the shares travelled from a low of HK$10.50 to a high of HK$107.20 and back to HK$38.70 — a rise of more than ten times, then a fall of 64% from the peak. The collapse was not gradual. The shares closed at HK$104.20 on 25 June 2026 and at HK$29.14 on 30 July 2026: a 72% loss in five weeks. Since then they have chopped violently between HK$29 and HK$42, including a 9% gain on 17 August followed by an 8% loss on 18 August. Daily volume through the crash ran 100–250 million shares against a 923 million share free float.

What that pattern says: the marginal buyer and seller here are not underwriting laminate margins. They are trading a theme. A shareholder register turning over at that speed provides no support at any particular price.

**The disclosure timing is a second signal.** The profit alert came on 30 July 2026, the day the shares bottomed at HK$29.14 after a five-week collapse. Whether or not that timing was deliberate, the practical effect was to put a very strong number into a very weak tape. The shares are 33% above that low three weeks later. An investor should be honest with themselves that they are now paying for information that has already been published.

**A quiet terminology point.** The market's framing of this company has shifted from "laminates" to "AI supply chain" without the company itself having reclassified anything. The reporting segments remain Laminates, Properties and Investments. The company has not, in its own disclosures, adopted the AI framing. That gap between how the market describes a business and how the business describes itself is usually worth respecting — the company knows what it sells.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING.** This is not a euphemism and it is not grudging. The operating business is genuinely inflecting: three consecutive halves of expanding gross margin, second-half 2025 profit up 152% year on year, and a company-issued alert that first-half 2026 profit more than tripled. Whoever underwrites the bear case must do so knowing the near-term numbers are going to be excellent.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** *The strength of the business and the attractiveness of the security are two different questions here, and they currently point in opposite directions.* At HK$38.70 the market values the equity at about HK$122 billion. That is roughly fifty times the last reported annual earnings, about seven and a half times book value, and — the comparison I would put in front of the committee — **roughly two and a half times the market value the same company commanded at the top of its last cycle in 2021, when it was earning HK$6.78 billion, a level the current consensus only expects it to reach again this year.** Buying this share today is not buying a recovery; it is buying an outcome better than the last peak, capitalised at a multiple this business has never sustained. The margin inflection is real. The price already assumes it continues, compounds, and re-rates.

**Economic moat: NARROW. Moat trend: STABLE.**

The moat type is **scale-cost**, extended by vertical integration into scarce upstream inputs — glass yarn and fabric, copper foil, epoxy resin, bleached kraft paper. That is a real advantage and it is structural: a competitor that must buy glass fabric on the spot market during a shortage cannot match the integrated producer's cost, and the fabric plants take years to build. It is not a switching-cost or network moat. Copper-clad laminate is qualified into customer designs but is fundamentally a specification-driven commodity, and the buyer set — large circuit-board manufacturers — is concentrated and sophisticated.

I judge the moat **narrow rather than wide**, and its trend **stable rather than widening**, on the returns evidence and against the explicit instruction that rising returns can indicate widening. Return on invested capital is 13.1% and return on equity 15.6%, both rising, and gross margin is expanding — the surface reading is "widening." I decline that reading for one reason: this exact set of indicators did the same thing into 2021, peaked at above 34% gross margin and roughly 30% return on equity, and then gave all of it back within eighteen months on the same asset base. Margin expansion driven by product price is a cycle, not a moat. What is durable here is the cost *position*, which has been stable for a decade and is neither widening nor eroding. Calling the moat "widening" on this evidence would be capitalising the cycle as though it were the franchise, which is precisely the error the 2021–2023 record warns against.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE.** There is no structural force impairing this company's terminal value. Quite the opposite — the direction of technology, toward higher layer-count, higher-frequency circuit boards for AI and networking hardware, increases both the volume and the specification of laminate required per unit. This is not a business being displaced. The threat that is real is competitive and cyclical rather than secular: Chinese overcapacity in materials is chronic, the current shortage in glass fabric and high-specification laminate is drawing capital toward exactly those bottlenecks, and the historical response time in this industry is roughly two to three years. That risk determines what the company earns in 2028; it does not determine whether the company exists.

**Fear-print or value trap? Neither — and this is the finding that matters most.** The framework the director will apply expects one of two answers: cheap because the market is afraid (a mispricing to buy) or cheap because the base is melting (a trap to avoid). This name is a third thing. It is **not cheap at all.** A share that has fallen 64% from its high is not thereby inexpensive; it is inexpensive *relative to its own recent mania*, which is not a valuation standard. On the last reported annual earnings of HK$0.78 the shares trade at roughly fifty times. On the average of a 2026 consensus whose high estimate is three times its low, they trade at fifteen times peak-cycle earnings — and paying fifteen times *peak* earnings for a commodity materials cyclical is not a margin of safety, it is a bet that this peak is a plateau. The crash is real, the business is strengthening, and the security is still expensive against any normalised earnings figure I can defend. Those three statements are all true simultaneously, and the director should not let the first two obscure the third.

Management credibility 3 of 5 · trajectory improving · a narrow but real moat · moat trend steady · structural threat manageable.

bull_thesis:
The bullish case rests on one genuine, verifiable claim: this company owns the actual bottleneck in the current electronics upcycle, and the numbers already show it. In a cycle where the scarce items are electronic-grade glass fabric and high-specification, low-loss laminate for artificial-intelligence server hardware, an integrated producer captures the margin of the entire chain rather than paying it away to suppliers. A competitor buying glass fabric on the spot market during a shortage simply cannot match that cost position, and new fabric capacity takes years to build.

The evidence that this is working is in the reported halves, not in a story. Gross margin has expanded sequentially across three consecutive reporting periods: 15.9% in the second half of 2024, 18.4% in the first half of 2025, 20.6% in the second half of 2025. Net income in the second half of 2025 was HK$1.51 billion against HK$598 million a year earlier, a rise of 152%. Then, on 30 July 2026, the company issued a positive profit alert stating that first-half 2026 profit would be more than triple the year-earlier figure, which implies something above HK$2.8 billion earned in six months, more than the whole of 2025. On the forward estimates, they do not: the five analysts covering the name model 2026 revenue of about HK$35.4 billion and average earnings per share of HK$2.58, rising to HK$3.50 in 2027 and HK$4.18 in 2028. At HK$38.70 that is fifteen times this year, eleven times next year and nine times the year after. If the artificial-intelligence build-out is a multi-year capital cycle rather than a two-year spike, and if the shift toward high-specification grades is a permanent mix improvement rather than a price blip, then a company earning HK$3.50 a share deserves more than eleven times, and the shares are worth double today's price.

The conditions this case depends on, stated plainly so they can be falsified: first, that high-speed laminate demand keeps growing through 2027 and 2028 rather than pausing when the first wave of data-centre orders is filled; second, that the glass-fabric and high-specification laminate shortage persists long enough that competitor capacity arriving in 2027-28 does not collapse pricing; third, that the mix shift toward specialty grades is durable enough to hold gross margin above the 20% level rather than reverting to the mid-teens; and fourth, that the poor cash conversion of 2025 proves to be an upcycle working-capital drain that unwinds, rather than a permanent feature of how this company sells.

Start with the precedent, because it is decisive. In 2021 Kingboard Laminates earned HK$6.78 billion on revenue of HK$28.80 billion, with gross margin above 34% and earnings per share of HK$2.17. That was the previous mania in laminate pricing. At HK$38.70 the equity is valued at about HK$122 billion, with enterprise value of roughly HK$124 billion once the HK$1.75 billion of net debt is added. The current consensus only expects it to earn HK$6.64 billion this year. In other words, the market is paying two and a half times the previous peak valuation for a business the street expects to merely match its previous peak profit.

The consensus itself will not bear the weight being put on it. Four analysts supply the 2026 earnings estimate, and their range is HK$1.25 to HK$3.74 a share — the highest is three times the lowest. Underwriting at the average means underwriting a number no individual analyst actually holds. At the low end of the 2026 range the shares trade at thirty-one times, not fifteen.

The forensic quality of the earnings is the second problem. Reported 2025 net income was HK$2.44 billion, but cash generated from operations across the two halves was only about HK$1.20 billion — roughly half. After HK$1.28 billion of capital spending, free cash flow for the year was approximately negative HK$80 million. A business whose profits do not convert to cash at the top of its cycle has a receivables book that is a risk, not an asset, when the cycle turns and customers come under pressure.

The third problem is the market environment. The dominant shared driver of this entire trade is artificial-intelligence capital spending, which is also the single most crowded macro factor in the current tape. The market has already begun to discriminate within that complex on the basis of free cash flow rather than revenue growth, and this company generated none in its last reported year. The share price itself has voted: HK$104.20 on 25 June 2026 to HK$29.14 on 30 July, a 72% loss in five weeks, followed by a violent chop between HK$29 and HK$42, with more than 9% of the entire free float trading on an average day. That is not a shareholder register that provides support at any particular level. With only 29% of the 3.15 billion shares in public hands and average daily volume of 83 million, this is a momentum battleground.

What would confirm the bear case: half-year results in late August that show the profit tripling as promised but with receivables extending further and operating cash flow still lagging profit; commentary or industry data showing new glass-fabric and high-specification laminate capacity being commissioned in China through 2027; a second-half order book that flattens rather than accelerates; or gross margin peaking below the 30% level the company reached in 2021, which would confirm that this cycle is smaller than the last one while the valuation assumes it is larger.

Where we disagree with the market is not about the earnings. It is about what those earnings are.

The street's position, expressed in the numbers, is that Kingboard Laminates earns about HK$2.58 a share in 2026, HK$3.50 in 2027 and HK$4.18 in 2028, and the twelve-month analyst target of HK$51.66 says those forecasts deserve roughly fifteen times. We think the first assumption is where the error sits, and this company's own accounts contain the refutation. In 2021 it earned HK$2.17 a share with gross margin above 34%. Eighteen months later, in the second half of 2022, half-year profit was HK$83 million and gross margin was 12%. By 2023, earnings per share were HK$0.29. Nothing structural changed — the same plants, the same vertical integration into glass, copper and resin, the same customers. Only the price of laminate changed. The street is currently modelling 2028 earnings per share of HK$4.18, which would be nearly double the highest annual figure this business has ever produced, at a point in the cycle when new capacity in exactly the bottleneck products is being financed. The historical response time for Chinese materials capacity is two to three years, which lands precisely on the 2028 forecast.

The second disagreement is about the consensus itself, and it is a disagreement about epistemics rather than about laminate. Four analysts supply the 2026 earnings estimate and their range is HK$1.25 to HK$3.74; for 2027 it is HK$1.45 to HK$5.42. When the highest estimate is three to four times the lowest, the average is not a forecast, it is a summary of confusion. Anyone underwriting at fifteen times the average is underwriting a number no individual analyst holds. At the low end of the 2026 range, today's price is thirty-one times earnings.

The third disagreement, and the one the current tape cares about most, is about cash. The market is valuing this company on reported profit. Reported 2025 net income was HK$2.44 billion; cash generated from operations was about HK$1.20 billion; after HK$1.28 billion of capital spending, free cash flow was approximately negative HK$80 million. Receivables of HK$9.21 billion represent about 165 days of sales and grew HK$1.83 billion in the second half of 2025 alone — more than that half's entire net income. The current market regime has explicitly begun to sort the artificial-intelligence complex on free cash flow rather than revenue growth, punishing the capital-spending payers while rewarding the cash generators. On that test this company scores badly, and we do not believe that is yet in the price.

Where we agree with the market, and it matters: the near-term earnings are going to be excellent, the margin inflection across three consecutive reported halves is real, and the vertical integration into glass fabric is a genuine advantage rather than a marketing line. We are not calling this a bad business. We are calling it a good business at a price that already assumes the best case.

But the honest assessment is that this event is unlikely to force a re-rating in our favour, because it is a catalyst for a thesis we do not hold. The magnitude has already been disclosed, and the shares have already risen 33% from their 30 July low in anticipation. What the announcement will genuinely reveal, and what nobody outside the company currently knows, are four things: the interim dividend, whether operating cash flow finally converted a reasonable share of the reported profit, whether the receivables balance extended beyond 165 days of sales, and any commentary on the second-half order book and on the product mix between commodity and high-specification grades. Those are the disclosures that would move our view, and three of the four could plausibly move it further against the stock rather than toward it.

The event that would actually force the re-rating this valuation implies is a slower one, and it is a de-rating rather than a re-rating: the arrival, most likely through 2027, of new Chinese capacity in electronic-grade glass fabric and high-specification laminate, and the consequent normalisation of the pricing that has produced the current margin expansion. The industry's historical capacity response time is two to three years from the onset of a shortage, which lands on the period the current consensus expects to be the strongest. There is no single dated announcement for that; it arrives as a sequence of reported half-years in which the margin stops improving. That is the eighteen-month horizon on which our base case sits.

One further consideration under this book's rules on independence of drivers. The resolution driver for this entire thesis — artificial-intelligence capital spending — is the single most dominant shared macro factor in the current market, and the regime framework requires that concentration in one such factor be enforced against rather than accumulated. Whatever forces this stock's next move, it will very likely be the same thing that moves every other name in that complex on the same day, which is precisely the kind of exposure this book is meant to avoid stacking.
valley_of_death:
The risky window here is unusual, because the near-term news is likely to be good and the risk is that good news is not enough.

Within two weeks, on or before 31 August 2026, the half-year results arrive. They will almost certainly show profit more than tripling, because the company said so on 30 July. The specific danger is that the market has already paid for that: the shares have risen 33% from their 30 July low of HK$29.14 to today's HK$38.70 on precisely this expectation. The most likely near-term disappointment is not the headline but the quality beneath it — an operating cash-flow line that again converts only about half of reported profit, a receivables balance extending beyond the 165 days already on the books, or a smaller-than-hoped interim dividend given that the 2025 payout of HK$1.93 billion already exceeded that year's free cash flow and was accompanied by HK$901 million of new short-term borrowing. Any of those would confirm the bear's core forensic point at exactly the moment sentiment is most stretched.

Over the following three to nine months the harder problem arrives. This is a business with a working-capital hump, not a cash-burn hump: in an upcycle where both volumes and prices rise, receivables and inventory absorb cash faster than profit produces it. That is precisely what happened in 2025, and 2026's much larger revenue base will make it worse in absolute terms. Capital spending is also running above depreciation — HK$1.28 billion against roughly HK$1.0 billion of depreciation in 2025, a ratio of about 1.37 — because the company is adding the capacity the shortage justifies. The combination means free cash flow can stay negative through a boom, and the dividend can only be sustained by borrowing against it. There is no maturity wall and no solvency question; net debt is under one turn of operating profit before depreciation and the solvency score is 9.5. But a company that cannot self-fund its dividend at the top of its cycle has no cash cushion to deploy when the cycle turns.

The macro overlay is the sharpest near-term risk. The current regime read describes a market in which the artificial-intelligence complex has split in half, with the capital-spending payers being destroyed while a narrow set of component suppliers melts up, and in which free cash flow rather than revenue has become the discriminator. It also warns explicitly that the recent promotion of freshly crashed names as an attractive hunting ground rests on selection of the three winners of a two-week window, with no accounting for the crashes that simply kept crashing. This name is a freshly crashed, negative-free-cash-flow, artificial-intelligence-capital-spending supply-chain stock. It sits on the wrong side of every one of those distinctions. Separately, the regime notes the September rate decision now carries roughly a 30-34% probability of a hike and zero probability of a cut through December; a higher-for-longer path is not friendly to a stock trading at fifty times trailing earnings.

Finally, the sheer volatility is itself a risk to any position taken now. In the last five weeks the shares have moved from HK$104.20 (25 June) to HK$29.14 (30 July), then chopped between HK$29 and HK$42, including a 9% gain on 17 August immediately followed by an 8% fall on 18 August. A position sized as though this were an ordinary industrial holding would be sized wrong by a wide margin.
positioning_washout:
The shareholder register here is the opposite of the yield-focused, passive base this question usually contemplates, and that changes the answer entirely.

Only about 29% of the 3.15 billion shares are in public hands — roughly 923 million shares — with the balance held by Jamplan (BVI) Limited, the holding vehicle of the wider Kingboard group. Average daily volume is about 83 million shares, and through the crash it ran between 100 million and 250 million a day, peaking at 318 million on 17 June. On a typical day, in other words, roughly 9% of the entire free float changes hands; on the worst days, more than a quarter of it. That is not an investment register. It is a trading venue.

The practical consequence is that there is no mechanical forced-selling event to wait for, because the forced selling has already happened and it happens continuously. The 72% collapse from HK$104.20 on 25 June to HK$29.14 on 30 July, in five weeks and on enormous volume, was the wash-out. Anyone who was going to be liquidated by margin calls or momentum-strategy stop-outs has largely been liquidated. What remains is a fast-turning base of traders positioned around the half-year results, and that base provides no support at any particular price — it will not defend HK$38, and it did not defend HK$60 or HK$80 on the way down.

This matters for how the committee should think about the entry level. In a normal deep-value situation you can wait for a capitulation and buy the last seller. Here, the capitulation already came and went in July and the shares are 33% above that low, so waiting for the flush is waiting for something that has already occurred. The flush that would actually create an opportunity is a second, valuation-driven de-rating rather than a positioning-driven one — the kind that arrives when the earnings are still rising but the multiple stops being paid, which is what happened to this company through 2022. That is a slower and less dramatic process than a five-week collapse, and it does not announce itself with a volume spike.

One structural point cuts the other way and should be acknowledged. A 29% free float in a name with a genuine thematic story is a squeeze mechanism. There is very little stock available relative to the demand a theme can generate, which is a large part of why the shares went from HK$10.50 to HK$107.20 in the first place. The same mechanism can run again on a strong interim print. That is a reason to expect further violent upside episodes; it is not a reason to own the shares at a price above our estimate of what the business is worth.
moderator_conclusion:
Pass for now, at conviction 2, and we are inheriting that call from our own decision of 10 August rather than re-deriving it, because nothing dated has happened in the business since then that would justify changing it. The half-year results have still not been published, the 30 July profit alert remains the most recent company statement, and the only thing that has moved is the price — HK$35.72 then, HK$38.70 now. A higher price on unchanged facts makes the case slightly worse.

Let us be precise about what we are and are not saying, because the temptation to read this as a bearish view of the company would be a misreading. This is a good business having a genuinely good year. Kingboard Laminates is the world's largest maker of copper-clad laminate, the fibreglass-and-copper sheet underneath every printed circuit board, and it is unusual in that it makes its own copper foil, glass yarn, glass fabric and resin rather than buying them. In a cycle where electronic-grade glass fabric is the scarce item, that integration is worth real money, and the accounts show it: gross margin has expanded across three consecutive reported halves, from 15.9% to 18.4% to 20.6%, and second-half 2025 profit rose 152% year on year. The company told the market in writing on 30 July 2026 that first-half 2026 profit would be more than triple the prior year. The balance sheet is genuinely conservative — net debt of about HK$1.75 billion is under one turn of operating profit before depreciation, and the solvency score of 9.5 leaves no financial distress question. Our forensic review scored management's credibility at 3 out of 5 and the business trajectory as strengthening, with a narrow but real cost moat that is stable rather than widening, and no structural force threatening the company's long-term existence.

Our objection is entirely about price, and it comes down to one comparison. At HK$38.70 the market values this equity at about HK$122 billion. At the top of its last cycle in 2021, when it actually earned HK$6.78 billion — a figure the street only expects it to match this year — the same company was worth roughly two-fifths of that. We are being asked to pay two and a half times the previous peak valuation for a business expected to merely match its previous peak profit, in an industry whose last peak was followed by an 87% earnings collapse within two years on an unchanged asset base. Valuing the business by its parts, we get to about HK$22 a share: roughly HK$22.00 from the laminates and upstream materials operations on normalised earnings of HK$2.20 a share at ten times, plus about HK$0.40 for the property and long-term investment portfolio marked down for Chinese property weakness, less about HK$0.56 for net debt. Our adverse case is HK$12 and our favourable case is HK$49. The price today sits above our base case and below our best case, which is the worst possible place to be underwriting: no margin of safety, and roughly two and a half times as much distance to the adverse case as to the favourable one. There is no structural floor to catch a fall — no net cash, no deal terms, no tender, and a book value of HK$5.20 that is nowhere near the price.

Three things reinforce the call. First, the earnings do not convert to cash: 2025 profit of HK$2.44 billion produced about HK$1.20 billion of operating cash flow and, after capital spending, roughly negative HK$80 million of free cash flow, with receivables at 165 days of sales and the dividend part-funded by new borrowing. The current market regime has begun sorting this entire complex on free cash flow rather than revenue, and on that test this name fails. Second, the analyst consensus being used to justify the price is unusable — four analysts with a 2026 estimate range of HK$1.25 to HK$3.74 a share are not forecasting, they are disagreeing, and at the low end today's price is thirty-one times earnings. Third, the resolution driver is artificial-intelligence capital spending, the single most crowded shared macro factor in this tape, and our own framework requires us to enforce independence of drivers rather than accumulate exposure to that one. The regime document also warns, in its own words, that the recent enthusiasm for freshly crashed names rests on selecting the winners of a two-week window without accounting for the crashes that kept crashing. This name is a freshly crashed, negative-cash-flow, artificial-intelligence-supply-chain stock; it is the exact profile that warning was written about.

We have deliberately not let the upcoming half-year announcement move the score in either direction. Under this book's rules the timing of a corporate event is descriptive, not a conviction lever — the dated-event portfolio is run separately — so what we are judging here is the residual value case, and that case is unattractive at HK$38.70 regardless of what happens on 31 August. By the same token we are not penalising the name for the fact that the profit figure has already been pre-announced.

What would change our mind, stated as a level rather than a hope: a price in the low twenties or below, which would put the shares at our base-case value with the operating momentum still intact, or evidence in the interim results and the following period that cash conversion has genuinely normalised — operating cash flow at or above reported profit and receivables days falling meaningfully below 150 — which would let us raise normalised earnings and the multiple together. Absent one of those, this is a business we admire at a price we decline.

# Kingboard Laminates Holdings (1888.HK): a deep dive on management and the setup

**As of 2026-10-26. Price used: HK$35.98 (Hong Kong listing, HKD close 2026-10-26, Yahoo Finance delayed quote; the paid FMP data connector was not responding this session).**

**Source limits, stated up front.** No earnings-call transcript was bundled, the FMP transcript and quote tools timed out, the company's investor-relations site refused the connection, and this session's web-search budget had run out. Kingboard Laminates does not hold Western-style quarterly calls in any case: it reports twice a year (interim results in August, full-year results in March) through Hong Kong exchange filings. So this dossier works from the hard numbers, the share-price record and the few dated headlines that could be fetched. It contains no management quotes, because none could be sourced, and none are invented.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story is a cyclical upswing that the market turned into an AI story. Kingboard Laminates makes copper-clad laminate (CCL: the copper-and-glass-fibre sheet that printed circuit boards are etched from), and the wider Kingboard group also makes its own copper foil, glass yarn and resin.

- **2021 to 2023, the down-leg.** Revenue fell from HK$28.8B (2021) to HK$16.75B (2023) and net profit from HK$6.78B to HK$0.91B. Earnings per share (EPS) fell from HK$2.17 to HK$0.29. That is an ordinary commodity-electronics downturn: consumer-electronics destocking plus lower copper-linked selling prices.
- **2024 to 2025, the recovery.** Revenue grew to HK$18.54B and then HK$20.40B; EPS went to HK$0.42 and then HK$0.78. Gross margin widened from about 16% (2023) to 19.6% (2025).
- **2026, the AI re-rating.** Trailing-twelve-month (TTM) figures to mid-2026 show revenue of HK$25.7B, gross profit of HK$6.81B (a 26.5% margin) and net profit of HK$4.40B, with diluted EPS of HK$1.39 (Yahoo Finance). The shares went from about HK$13 at the end of 2025 to a closing high of HK$104.20 on 2026-06-25, an eightfold move. A GuruFocus headline from about four months ago framed it as an "AI rally" with mainland Chinese investors doubling their stake.
- **July 2026 onward, the round trip.** The stock fell from HK$99.15 (2026-06-30) to HK$29.14 (2026-07-30), down about 71% in a month. A GuruFocus headline from about three months ago linked a delay to Nvidia's next server rack ("Kyber") to weakness across Asian AI suppliers, with Kingboard tagged. The shares bounced to about HK$55 in early October and have since slid to HK$35.98.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

With no management commentary available, the "claims" tested here are the market's.

| Earnings are inflecting hard | TTM net profit HK$4.40B against HK$2.44B for 2025, so the latest half roughly doubled on the year before. The screener shows the latest period's EPS up about 296% year on year. | Matches |

The screener's own value models (discounted cash flow, earnings-power value, Graham, owner earnings) all put the stock 74% to 100% above fair value. Those models are backward-looking and anchored on weaker 2025 cash flow, but they agree in direction.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

This cannot be rated from management's words because no transcript or commentary could be sourced. The financial trajectory is rising: three straight periods of improving revenue, margin and profit. The market's tone has swung from euphoric (June) to fearful (July) and back to cautious.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

Not assessable. Kingboard Laminates historically gives little or no numerical guidance, and none could be verified for 2026. Reliability: unrated. The interim dividend record shows a HK$0.15 payment in December 2025 and a HK$0.53 payment in June 2026 (ex-dividend dates from the price history). A dividend that rises more than threefold is a concrete sign that the board trusts the upswing.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

No consensus estimates or price targets could be found: Yahoo's analysis page was empty and FMP has no target coverage for this listing. These are the questions a reader should press:
- How much of the 2026 margin jump is price increases passed on ahead of copper costs, which reverse when copper eases, and how much is high-end AI laminate, which could last?
- What share of revenue is high-speed, low-loss laminate for AI servers, compared with mainstream FR-4 board (the standard grade for ordinary electronics)?
- How exposed is the order book to the timing of one customer's product roadmap, given that the July sell-off followed a reported Nvidia rack delay?
